newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania, German police sign accord to fight crime.
newsitem.headline: Romania, German police sign accord to fight crime.

text.p: Romania and Germany agreed on Tuesday to fight organised crime, on the rise since the end of communism, particularly a wave of safe-crackings in Germany and the use of Romania as a drugs trade route.
Interior ministry officials signed an accord to coordinate efforts in drugs and gun trafficking, money laundering, terrorism, counterfeiting and illegal migration.

German Deputy Interior Minister Kurt Schelter told reporters the Federal Crime Office in Karlsruhe would appoint a liaison officer in Bucharest "to contribute to world efforts to deal with this international plague".
The accord also provides for an exchange of data on suspects in crimes committed in the two countries.
The December 1989 anti-communist revolt opened Romania's borders after 50 years of isolation, generating new types of crime committed by foreigners here and by Romanians abroad.

Germany has proved to be one of most popular destinations for Romanians now able to travel freely. But Romanian officials say tens of thousands, mainly Gypsies, have been expelled for crossing the border illegally and large numbers have been convicted of a variety of offences.
The Germans are worried about the "safe-crackers" operation in which hundreds of often very heavy safes have been emptied in post offices or shops or pillaged in wooded areas.
German media alleged that the "crackers" were trained by members of executed Communist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu's disbanded Securitate secret police. Romanian officials deny the allegation.
"The 'safe cracker phenomena' is purely Romanian and we have arrested so far dozens of such criminals but have not yet clarified what is behind these gangs," Schelter said.
Romania is also coping with increased drug offences, made worse by the Bosnia war, which cut off traditional supply routes from the Middle East through former Yugoslavia.
Police this year have confiscated 4,700 kg (10,300 pounds) of various drugs, including 59 kg (130 pounds) of heroin and 130 kg (286 pounds) of cocaine.
